blocks.text: A priority queue is not really a data structure so much as it is a promise. It promises that no matter how many elements you throw at it, you can always retrieve the most important one immediately, and add a new one without paying the cost of resorting everything from scratch.

This lesson assumes you already understand how a heap works internally, sift up, sift down, and heapify are covered in Introduction to Heaps. Here the focus shifts from mechanics to design: how do you reach for a priority queue when a problem calls for it, how do you decide between a min heap and a max heap, and how do the two most common priority queue patterns, K largest elements and merging K sorted lists, actually work in practice.
By the end of this lesson you should be able to look at a problem statement and immediately recognize the shape of a priority queue problem, then pick the right flavor of heap without hesitating.
Strip away the implementation details and a priority queue is defined purely by its interface, the set of operations it guarantees and the time each one costs.

items: Insert: add a new element in O(log n) time
Peek: look at the highest priority element without removing it in O(1) time
Extract: remove and return the highest priority element in O(log n) time

blocks.text: Notice what is missing from that list: there is no promise that the entire collection is sorted, and no promise about how quickly you can find an arbitrary element buried in the middle. A priority queue is deliberately narrow. It only cares about the one element sitting at the top, and it is willing to reorganize itself just enough to keep answering that one question quickly.

The word priority is doing a lot of work here. Priority can mean smallest, largest, earliest deadline, highest frequency, or any other ordering you define with a comparator. The abstract interface stays identical regardless of what priority means for your specific problem, only the comparator changes.
A priority queue does not promise sorted output as you go. It promises fast access to whichever single element currently matters most: insert in O(log n), peek in O(1), and extract in O(log n).

content.title: 2. Why a Heap is the Standard Backing Structure

blocks.text: If all a priority queue needs to do is hand you the top element quickly and accept new elements quickly, several data structures could technically do the job. So why does virtually every implementation, including C++'s std::priority_queue, choose a heap as the backing structure?

Consider a sorted array first. Peeking at the smallest or largest element is O(1) because it always sits at one end. But inserting a new element means finding the correct position and shifting every element after it, an O(n) operation in the worst case. For a data structure meant to absorb a continuous stream of insertions, that cost is unacceptable.

A plain binary search tree looks more promising on paper: insert, and extract the minimum or maximum, can all run in O(log n) if the tree stays balanced. The catch is the phrase if the tree stays balanced. An unbalanced BST degrades toward a linked list, with O(n) operations. Getting that O(log n) guarantee back requires extra machinery, AVL rotations or red black coloring rules, that exist purely to keep the tree from leaning too far in one direction.

A heap sidesteps all of that. Its shape property forces it to always be a complete binary tree, which by construction has height O(log n) with no rebalancing logic required. Its heap property guarantees the element you care about, the minimum or the maximum, always sits at the root, so peek is O(1). Because it lives in a flat array with simple index arithmetic instead of pointers, it also has excellent cache behavior compared to a pointer chasing BST.

blocks.text: This is the sense in which a heap gets O(log n) bounds for free. It doesn't need rotations, color bits, or complex rebalancing invariants, just two simple structural rules that are trivial to maintain during insert and extract.

content.title: 3. Min Heap vs Max Heap in C++

blocks.text: In C++, std::priority_queue defaults to a max heap. Call top() and you get the largest element currently in the queue, not the smallest. This surprises a lot of people coming from languages where the default leans the other way.

Plenty of problems, K largest elements being the prime example, actually need a min heap. C++ does not give you a separate min-priority-queue type. Instead you flip the ordering by supplying two extra template arguments.

The full template signature is priority_queue<T, Container, Compare>. The first argument, T, is the element type. The second, Container, is the underlying container that actually stores the elements, almost always vector<T>. The third, Compare, is the comparator that decides ordering.

By default Compare is less<T>, which sounds like it should produce ascending order but actually produces a max heap, because the priority queue interprets less as meaning this element belongs lower in priority, pushing larger elements toward the top. Swapping in greater<T> inverts that logic, so now smaller elements are treated as higher priority and rise to the top.

The order of these three template arguments is fixed and you cannot skip the middle one. Writing priority_queue<int, greater<int>> without specifying the container will not compile, since the compiler expects the second slot to be a container type, not a comparator.

Quick memory aid: priority_queue<int> alone is a max heap. To get a min heap, spell out all three template arguments and swap in greater<int> for the comparator: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>.

One of the most common reasons to reach for a priority queue is the K largest elements pattern, sometimes phrased as K smallest or K most frequent, but always structurally the same problem: from a large collection, or an unbounded stream, identify the K elements that matter most, without fully sorting everything.

The brute force option is to sort the entire collection and slice off the last K elements. That costs O(n log n) regardless of how small K is. If n is a million and K is 10, you are paying for a full sort just to throw away almost everything you sorted.
A priority queue lets you avoid sorting the parts you don't need. The trick, and the part that trips people up, is that finding the K largest elements uses a min heap, not a max heap.

Here is the reasoning. You maintain a heap that is only ever allowed to hold K elements, your current best guess at the answer. At any point, the element you are least confident about, the one most likely to get kicked out by a better candidate, is the smallest element currently in your heap of K. To find that weakest candidate instantly so you can compare it against a new incoming element, you need the smallest one sitting at the top, which is exactly what a min heap gives you.

items: Push every incoming element onto the min heap
If the heap size exceeds K, pop the top, this discards the current smallest of your K candidates
After processing every element, the heap holds exactly the K largest values seen so far

blocks.text: A max heap of size K would do the opposite of what you want here, it would keep discarding your largest candidates and leave you holding the K smallest instead. This is the single most common source of confusion when people first meet this pattern, so it is worth internalizing the rule directly: for K largest, use a min heap sized to K, and for K smallest, use a max heap sized to K.

content.title: 5. Worked Trace: Finding the 3 Largest From a Stream

blocks.text: Let's trace through an actual stream to make the min heap of size K approach concrete. Suppose numbers arrive one at a time in this order: 5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, and we want the 3 largest values seen by the end. K is 3, so our min heap is never allowed to hold more than 3 elements.

blocks.text: After all six elements have streamed through, the min heap settled on {5, 8, 9}, exactly the 3 largest values in the input. Notice that 1 and 3 never survived past the moment they were compared against the current smallest of the top 3, and 2 was evicted the instant a larger candidate, 9, arrived.

blocks.caption: The min heap of size 3 shrinks and grows as the stream 5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3 is processed, always keeping the 3 strongest candidates seen so far.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865495-646204475.png
blocks.alt: Worked Trace: Finding the 3 Largest From a Stream

blocks.text: This is the entire pattern in miniature: the min heap never grows past size K, and every element that enters either survives by pushing out something weaker, or gets discarded immediately because it was never competitive to begin with.

Because the heap never exceeds size K, this approach works even when the input is an unbounded stream that would never fit in memory as a full array. You only ever pay O(K) space, no matter how many elements pass through.

content.title: 6. C++ Implementation and Complexity: K Largest Elements

blocks.text: Here is the pattern translated directly into C++, using std::priority_queue as the min heap.

The loop is exactly the pattern described earlier: push every element, and whenever the heap grows past size k, pop the top to discard the weakest of the current top k candidates. One subtle bonus, when you drain a min heap at the end by repeatedly popping, the values come out in ascending order for free, since pop always removes the current minimum.

Each push and pop on a heap of size K costs O(log K). Since the heap never exceeds size K throughout the entire scan, and there are n elements to process, the total cost is O(n log K). Compare that to sorting the whole array first, which costs O(n log n) regardless of how small K is.

The difference matters most when K is much smaller than n. Suppose n is one million and K is 10. Sorting the full array costs roughly n log n comparisons, on the order of twenty million. The heap approach costs roughly n log K, on the order of three to four million, since log base 2 of 10 is only about 3.3. That is nearly a six times reduction in work, and the gap widens further as K shrinks relative to n.

A second extremely common priority queue pattern is merging K sorted lists into one sorted output. It appears whenever you have several independently sorted sources, K sorted log files, K sorted search result pages, or K sorted linked lists, and you need one combined sorted stream.

A naive way to merge K lists is to merge them two at a time, repeatedly combining the result with the next list. This can be shown to cost roughly O(n times K) in the worst case, since every element may get re-compared as the merged list keeps growing across K successive passes. It also does not use a priority queue at all.

The heap based approach is faster and conceptually cleaner. The core idea is to always know the smallest available element across all K lists at once, without re-scanning every list's current head on every step.

items: Push the first element, or the head node, of every one of the K lists onto a min heap
Pop the minimum, this is guaranteed to be the next element of the final merged output
Push whatever element comes immediately after the one you just popped, from that same list, back onto the heap
Repeat until the heap is empty

blocks.text: At every moment, the heap holds at most one candidate per list, so its size never exceeds K. Its top is always the smallest element among everything currently available, which is exactly the next element the merged output needs.

blocks.caption: The min heap holds exactly one live candidate from each of the K lists at a time. Popping the smallest and pushing that list's next element keeps the invariant intact.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865495-788333864.png

This is the same push then pop then push again rhythm used in the K largest pattern, just wired up differently. Instead of discarding the loser, here you replace the winner, the element you just popped, with its successor from the same list.

Let n be the total number of elements across all K lists combined, and K be the number of lists. Every element is pushed exactly once and popped exactly once, and each of those operations costs O(log K) because the heap never holds more than K elements at a time. That gives a total time of O(n log K), a clear improvement over the O(n times K) pairwise approach once K grows past a handful of lists.

Most bugs in priority queue code are not algorithmic mistakes, they are small mechanical slips that produce code which compiles and runs but returns the wrong answer. These are worth memorizing precisely because they fail silently.

items: Using a max heap when the K largest pattern actually needs a min heap, or the reverse for K smallest, this silently produces the wrong K elements rather than crashing, which makes it dangerous in an interview setting
Forgetting the greater<int> comparator in C++ and assuming priority_queue<int> behaves like a min heap by default, when it is actually a max heap

Pushing custom objects or structs into a priority_queue without defining operator< or supplying a custom comparator, which either fails to compile or, worse, compiles but silently orders elements incorrectly if the comparator logic is subtly wrong
Confusing the size of the heap with the size of the input, the heap in these patterns is intentionally bounded to K, not to n
Forgetting to handle empty lists when seeding a K way merge, pushing a head from a list that has zero elements leads to reading past the end of that list

blocks.text: Notice the comparator functor itself uses operator>. A comparator supplied to priority_queue answers the question does a belong strictly below b in priority, so returning true when a.val is greater than b.val is what produces a min heap ordering. This inversion catches almost everyone off guard the first time they write one.

When in doubt, write a quick two step test: push three known values into your comparator and print top() before writing the rest of your solution. It costs seconds and catches the max versus min mixup immediately.
Once the min versus max heap choice feels automatic, here are real interview problems that draw directly on the patterns covered in this lesson.

items: Easy Kth Largest Element in a Stream, maintain a running min heap of size K across repeated calls
Medium Kth Largest Element in an Array, the canonical fixed size min heap of size K problem
Hard Merge k Sorted Lists, the direct linked list version of the merge K sorted lists pattern
Medium Top K Frequent Elements, combine a frequency map with a heap of size K, ordered by frequency instead of value
Hard Find Median from Data Stream, a related but more advanced two heap pattern, one max heap for the lower half and one min heap for the upper half, worth its own dedicated lesson

blocks.text: That last one deserves a mention even though it goes beyond a single priority queue: balancing two heaps against each other to track a running median builds directly on everything covered here, so it is a natural next stop once this pattern feels comfortable.
Before walking into an interview or a real design discussion, make sure you can answer each of these without pausing to rederive it from scratch.

items: Can you state the three operations a priority queue guarantees, and their time complexities, without hesitating?
Given a K largest versus K smallest problem, can you immediately name the correct heap type without working it out from scratch each time?
Do you know the exact C++ syntax to declare a min heap, including why the container argument cannot be skipped?
Can you explain why a bounded heap of size K gives O(n log K) instead of O(n log n), and why that matters when K is much smaller than n?
Can you implement the merge K sorted lists pattern from scratch, including correctly pushing the next element from whichever list you just popped from?
If you push a custom struct into a priority_queue, do you know how to define a correct comparator, and can you explain why the comparator's logic feels inverted for a min heap?

blocks.text: Once these questions feel automatic, the two follow up lessons, the Top K Elements pattern and K Way Merge with Heaps, go much deeper into edge cases and additional variations built on exactly this foundation.
